strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear formalization of 'decisive error recognition' in MAS; strong empirical observation that >80% of failures exhibit high semantic similarity enables practical knowledge transfer
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 model families and diverse datasets with solid ablation studies demonstrating robustness to cache size and schema count variations

Practical training-free framework suitable for dynamic MAS deployments; addresses real operational constraints (32K+ token trajectories, computational efficiency) not adequately handled by prior methods
Valuable CORRECT-Error dataset contribution with novel error injection pipeline; human evaluation shows synthetic errors are effectively indistinguishable from real ones (47% misclassified)
Consistent improvements across diverse tasks (+20% on WHO&WHEN, +17-28% average on CORRECT-Error) with effective transfer of schemas across datasets and models
weaknesses: Schema quality assurance critically underspecified: No human evaluation of schema quality itself, unclear how 'filtering/distillation' enforcement works (Algorithm 1), no analysis of how schema errors propagate to final predictions, missing specification of δ and θ_hot thresholds

Clustering methodology lacks essential details: No specification of similarity threshold, cluster count statistics, or sensitivity analysis—despite being central to schema extraction efficiency claims

Generalization claims insufficiently validated: All evaluated datasets are QA/reasoning variants; no testing on truly new domains (code generation, system control). Figure 6 shows only cross-variant transfer, not cross-domain generalization

Task-dependent impact undermines broad applicability: GAIA shows only +1.6 points improvement (28.6%→30.6%), baseline accuracy varies wildly (3.5%-38%), high variance in model performance not explained; Acc@1-5 metrics are loose for practical debugging

Reproducibility severely limited: GPT-5 required for schema generation (closed-source), CORRECT-Error synthesis cost 3B tokens from proprietary models, hyperparameter selection process not described, no code release mentioned

Moderate originality: Combines existing techniques (semantic clustering, retrieval-augmented prompting, LLM prompting) without fundamental innovation; heavily builds on Zhang et al. (2025) formulation with primarily engineering improvements

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem in MAS error recognition with clear motivation and well-validated core insight (>80% errors share semantic similarity >0.8)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with consistent improvements (17-28% gains) across multiple models, datasets, and thorough ablations demonstrating robustness
Training-free approach with minimal overhead (<3.5%) is valuable for real-world deployment with evolving error distributions, avoiding expensive retraining
Useful dataset contribution (CORRECT-Error: 2,000+ trajectories) with well-designed error-injection pipeline and human-alignment validation (52.9% unanimous consensus)
Careful experimental design including proper data leakage prevention, cross-domain transfer analysis, and streaming adaptation evaluation
Clear presentation with informative examples, well-structured methodology, and comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (standard LLM prompting for schema generation, cosine similarity retrieval, context-guided prompting) without substantial algorithmic innovation

Fundamental label quality problem: >50% disagreement rates on WHO&WHEN and acknowledged inherent subjectivity of decisive errors undermines evaluation reliability; paper inadequately addresses label ambiguity impact
Modest absolute performance: exact-step accuracy only 17.2% (GPT-5) on WHO&WHEN even with CORRECT; much higher tolerant metrics (Acc@5: 58.8%) suggest approximate rather than precise localization

Schema quality validation insufficient: schemas generated via LLM prompting with minimal analysis beyond downstream performance; schema distillation relies on ambiguous error labels (circular reasoning)

Retrieval mechanism under-explored: acknowledged that semantic similarity may not be optimal; no exploration of structured retrieval incorporating agent roles, tool dependencies, or causality; hard-negative robustness doesn't validate optimality

Limited domain diversity: all CORRECT-Error tasks focus on reasoning/QA (HotpotQA, Math500, MMLU-Pro); unclear generalization to software engineering, robotics, or structurally different MAS applications
Multi-error trajectory failure mode identified (Appendix A.11) but not addressed; frequency of occurrence not quantified

Reproducibility concerns: heavy dependence on proprietary GPT-5 for schema generation and specific model combinations (Magnetic-One, AutoGen) with incomplete configuration details; BAAI-BPE-M3 embedding model dependency
Synthetic data authenticity marginal: ~47% misclassification rates between synthetic and genuine errors suggest synthetic data may lack subtle distinguishing patterns
Insufficient analysis of failure modes and success conditions: no systematic study of which error types CORRECT handles well vs. poorly; limited case studies

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing error localization in multi-agent systems with clear practical importance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10+ LLM models and 7+ datasets with reasonable ablation studies
Useful dataset contribution (CORRECT-Error with 2,000+ annotated trajectories) and thoughtful error injection pipeline
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging subjectivity in error labels and unclear retrieval signals
Practical framework design with dynamic schema management (expansion/distillation) for deployment
Consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks and models, with strong cross-domain transferability shown in ablations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies standard clustering, semantic retrieval, and LLM-based summarization with minimal algorithmic innovation
Overstated claims about being 'lightweight' and 'training-free' when schema generation relies on expensive GPT-5 and introduces multiple hyperparameters (δ, θ_hot) requiring tuning
Modest absolute performance: best exact-step accuracy is 17.2%; even Acc@1 tops out at 32%, raising questions about practical utility

Insufficient schema quality validation: no quantitative evaluation of what % of ground-truth error patterns schemas capture; only one generic example provided; acknowledged gap vs. human-curated taxonomies

Unvalidated core assumptions: error repeatability assumption validated only on small WHO&WHEN dataset (~200 trajectories); decisive error definition requires knowing corrected alternative s̃_k at test time without discussion of how to obtain it
Weak baseline comparisons: LLM-as-a-judge strawman uses full trajectories; missing comparisons to causal analysis, binary search, and stronger error detection methods
Substantial oracle gap: CORRECT reaches only 71.5% of oracle performance using ground-truth trajectory-specific schemas, indicating fundamental limitations of retrieval-based approach
Synthetic data concerns: 47.1% of synthetic errors misclassified as genuine may indicate distribution mismatch; error injection based on learned schemas may miss novel failure modes
Missing statistical significance testing despite low absolute accuracy numbers; no error bars or confidence intervals reported
Incomplete computational cost analysis; claims of 'negligible overhead' not rigorously justified given GPT-5 dependency and lack of end-to-end cost comparison

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine operational needs in MAS debugging with clear evidence of error reusability (80% semantic similarity)
Practical, training-free framework deployable at inference-time with minimal overhead (<3.5%), enabling adaptation to dynamic error types without retraining
Comprehensive experimental validation across 7 datasets, multiple model architectures, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements (up to 19.8% on WHO&WHEN, 28.7% average)
Strong schema transferability validated across domains, model upgrades, and streaming-style adaptation scenarios
High-quality CORRECT-Error dataset with rigorous human validation (94.4% synthetic errors judged as genuine by multiple annotators), providing valuable benchmark for community
Robust to practical challenges including context truncation, retrieval noise, and hyperparameter variations
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging subjectivity of error labels and gaps in oracle comparison
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (semantic clustering, LLM-as-generator, retrieval) are well-established; contribution is primarily algorithmic combination and application rather than fundamental innovation
Modest absolute accuracies remain concerning for production deployment (WHO&WHEN Hand-Crafted: 17.2% Acc@0 with GPT-5), limiting independent deployment utility without human review
Schema generation quality insufficiently analyzed: entirely dependent on GPT-5 with no ablation on schema quality, no investigation of LLM bias or error propagation in generated schemata

Scalability and practical deployment concerns: cold-start performance degrades significantly, online expansion relies on user feedback (reliability unvalidated), schema distillation costs at scale undiscussed
Limited mechanistic understanding of schema transferability: paper lacks analysis of what structural properties enable cross-domain generalization despite claiming this as key insight
Subjectivity in decisive error labels acknowledged but unresolved: training/evaluation stability under label noise not addressed, despite >50% disagreement rates in prior work (WHO&WHEN)

Reproducibility contingencies: code URL blank, schema generation requires proprietary GPT-5 API access, CORRECT-Error pipeline requires specific infrastructure (Magentic-One, AutoGen), human evaluation lacks inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's kappa)
Unexplained performance variation across datasets: Math500 shows +46.9 point improvement while GAIA shows minimal gains; no analysis of factors driving these differences
Semantic similarity-based retrieval presented as robust but acknowledged as potentially suboptimal; no comparison to alternative retrieval methods (BM25, learned retrievers)
